For the collection of urine samples, a sterile, leak-proof container must be used. Whole urine samples can be transported in sealed containers at 4°C. 3. If facilities for processing or centrifuging urine samples are available, the sample should be stored at 4–8°C and centrifuged within 24 hours of collection. The centrifugation should be performed at 500 × g (approximately 1500 rpm) for 5–10 minutes, preferably at 4°C. After centrifugation, the supernatant must be removed. 4. To the sediment, sterile viral transport medium (VTM), tissue culture medium, or phosphate-buffered saline should be added to achieve a final volume of 2 mL. If no visible pellet is present, all but 1 mL of the liquid at the bottom of the centrifuge tube should be removed and mixed with an equal volume of VTM. 5. The processed urine sample should be stored at 4°C and shipped within 48 hours. Alternatively, the urine sample can be frozen at -70°C in VTM and transported on dry ice. 6. If storage at -70°C is not possible, samples can be stored at -20°C. While viral viability will be lost, the viral RNA integrity can still be maintained and detected via RT-PCR. 7. Regardless of the type of specimen collected, all specimens must reach the laboratory within five days of collection. 8. For antibody detection, a 1 mL blood sample should be collected. Alternatively, 5 mL of blood or dried blood spots (DBS) with at least three fully filled circles are acceptable. 9. Blood samples should be centrifuged to separate the serum, which should then be stored at 2–8°C for up to 24 hours or at 20–25°C for up to 6 hours. 10. Once clotting has occurred (either by spinning or allowing the sample to stand for 1 hour), the serum should be transferred to a sterile cryovial to prevent hemolysis. 11. Serum should be stored at 4–8°C until shipment, but not for longer than 7 days. If storage for more than 7 days is required, the serum should be frozen at -20°C or lower and transported to the testing laboratory on frozen ice packs. 12. For long-term storage, serum samples should be transported to the laboratory using a cold chain. Repeated freezing and thawing should be avoided as it can compromise the stability of IgM antibodies. 13. As a general rule, serum specimens should be shipped to the laboratory as soon as possible, and shipment should not be delayed for the collection of additional specimens. 14. Dried blood spots (DBS) can be used when venepuncture is not feasible or when a cold chain or cost-effective method for transporting serum samples is unavailable. 15. While venous blood can be used for DBS preparation, capillary blood is typically preferred. Blood should be collected by pricking a finger or heel with a sterile, single-use disposable lancet. 16. Blood spotted on filter paper should be allowed to air dry completely. Each card should be wrapped in wax paper and placed in a sealable plastic bag with a desiccant pack. 17. DBS should be stored at 4°C until they can be shipped to the laboratory. It is acceptable to transport DBS at ambient temperatures up to 42°C if they are delivered to the laboratory within 3 days. 18. For monitoring viral shedding in confirmed congenital rubella syndrome (CRS) cases, at least 80% of cases should demonstrate no longer shedding the virus. This is determined by at least two negative virus detection tests conducted at least one month apart in children aged ≤12 months. 19. For timely detection of CRS and congenital rubella infection (CRI) cases, at least 80% of cases should be identified within 3 months of birth. This includes cases found through active case searches. 20. Laboratory serological results should be reported within 4 days of specimen receipt in at least 80% of cases. This indicator applies only to public laboratories. 21. Dried blood spots can be transported at ambient temperatures up to 42°C if delivered to the laboratory within 3 days. Venous blood samples of 5 mL collected in sterile tubes are also acceptable for certain specimens, such as cerebrospinal fluid. 22. The completeness of monitoring for viral shedding and the timeliness of case detection and laboratory reporting are critical indicators for effective surveillance of vaccine-preventable diseases, particularly congenital rubella syndrome. 23. The document was developed under the strategic guidance of the WHO Regional Director and other key personnel, with contributions from various experts, including WHO consultants, country office staff, and external collaborators. 24. The technical content of the document was reviewed and updated by experts, including participants from a regional workshop held in June 2022, which included representatives from national immunization programs, WHO staff, UNICEF, and other collaborators.
